primary_claim: In a toy model with correlated features, the standard 'sparsity vs reconstruction tradeoff' is illusory: an SAE trained with L0 below the true underlying L0 achieves much better reconstruction than the ground-truth-matching SAE but does so by mixing correlated features into polysemantic latents ('feature hedging'), while only the SAE trained at the true L0 exactly recovers the true monosemantic features

effect.metric: reconstruction quality (variance explained/MSE) at different L0, trained vs. ground-truth SAE
effect.value: trained SAE at L0=1 achieves much better reconstruction than the ground-truth SAE (which exactly matches the 50 true features) but has polysemantic latents unrelated to the true features; the trained SAE at the true L0 (11) exactly matches the ground-truth SAE and perfectly recovers every true feature

contradicts_or_qualifies: the widely assumed 'sparsity vs reconstruction tradeoff' from prior SAE literature (e.g. Gao et al. 2024, arXiv:2406.04093), which implies better reconstruction always means a better SAE and that any reasonably low L0 is equally valid; this post shows both assumptions are wrong
stated_future_work: write a follow-up post on how to find the correct L0 for an SAE
limitations_stated: only demonstrated in a simple toy model with 50 features, not yet on real language-model SAEs
currently the only reliable way to find the correct L0 is to train a range of SAEs at different L0 parameters
does not discuss in this post how to find the correct L0 (deferred to the companion paper/a future post)
quote: Fundamentally, there is no "sparsity vs reconstruction tradeoff" - if the L0 of the SAE is not chosen correctly, the resulting SAE will be incorrect and polysemantic.
